thread.title: How Worried Would You Be If GM Had 25 Million Cars In Inventory? In A Way, They Do - General Motors Company (NYSE:GM)

author: Max Greve
title: How Worried Would You Be If GM Had 25 Million Cars In Inventory? In A Way, They Do - General Motors Company (NYSE:GM)
text:
I get ribbed a lot - some of it good-natured, others less so - about my articles on the car industry being “apocalyptic” and over the top, right down to their titles. It’s true I have an exceptionally bearish outlook on autos right now, but my titles aren’t meant to be apocalyptic or sensationalist. They are meant to highlight that people should be thinking about a problem in a different way.
No, GM doesn't have a hidden stash of 25 million unsold cars in some garage in the desert somewhere. But I believe the economic situation for the stock is much the same as if they did, and that is what I am trying to convey.
My Auto Transition Theory For some time now, I have been advocating a somewhat idiosyncratic theory on the auto market: not just that automotive transport will see a shift from auto ownership to ride-hailing, exemplified by Lyft ( LYFT ) and Uber ( UBER ) but that the shift will produce a drastic decline in total VMT(Vehicle Miles Travelled) and therefore, produce a permanent decline in the demand for autos from GM, Ford ( F ) and other auto companies.
My theory has already been covered in detail in several of my articles, and I won’t repeat it here: readers have all they need from me to form their own opinions, one way or the other. However, one thing that has repeatedly cropped up in the comments section is that even if I’m right - and most seem convinced I’m not - it will take too long for this effect to be felt, so it’s of no near-term relevance to investors in Toyota ( TM ) or Chrysler ( FCAU ) or anyone else.
I am only returning to this subject to explain, briefly, why that is absolutely not the case. Obviously we have had a good, strong debate about whether the auto industry really is heading for a major disruption, and there are differing views about that. But if I am right, there is absolutely no chance that it will take ten years, or even five years, to be felt by the auto manufacturers. Even if they are not feeling it already - and I believe the decline in auto sales from their peak is evidence that they are - the very structure and nature of our current personal automotive ecosystem is such that they must feel it soon.
Where The Inventory Really Lives Many analysts have discussed the potential losses for not just those auto companies and their finance arms, but also the banks like Citigroup ( C ) and Bank Of America ( BAC ) which finance many of the dealer inventory loans and also leases on cars - which will become dealer inventory again at some point - if they had to be liquidated in a fire sale. But far more significant than the fact that leases run for a couple of years, is the fact that cars run for a couple of decades .
The average life of a car is in excess of a decade. In fact the average age of a car right now is 11.4 years at last report. Meanwhile, the average auto production in the US is around 16-18 million units depending on the year. Each year that many cars give out - finally - and are replaced by new ones. So to have that replacement rate every year in a fleet of decade-old cars, the total size of the fleet has to be in the hundreds of millions, which of course we already know that it is.
What this means is that when we talk about “auto inventory” in the US, we miss the forest for the trees if we focus on the dealer inventory on the various lots owned by franchisees of GM, Ford, Honda ( HMC ) and all the rest. Even to focus on the leases, on the balance sheets of the auto manufacturers as well as the banks, is still to see only a small piece of the picture. By far, the largest source of auto inventory is the cars sitting on the general population’s lots, i.e., their driveways and apartment garages.
Transitioning To A Smaller Fleet As Lyft and Uber continue to expand and make car-sharing a viable alternative to car-ownership, I expect, as I have explained before, that the shift will produce a decline in VMT, owing to both more shared rides as well as a shift in the value perception of the marginal ride taken. That decline in VMT, in turn, must produce a decline in new car sales, since fewer VMT means fewer cars wear out and need replacing every year.
However, this is not the only effect the shift will have. The VMT is what might be considered the “permanent” effect, the thing that will impact car sales indefinitely and determine what the new equilibrium of the auto market will be. That effect, I agree, will take time to make itself fully felt, as new driving paradigms phase in over many years. There will be a transitional period.
But there will also be a transitional effect , a temporary dislocation of auto demand, as the level of car ownership goes down. Because of course people won’t just reduce how often they purchase replacement cars. They will also reduce how many cars are sitting in their driveway at any given time. That is, they will bleed off the inventory of cars they have already purchased, down to the new equilibrium level. And that transitional effect will be the mirror image of the permanent effect: it will be front-loaded and very heavy in the transitional period, before tailing off to nothing when the new equilibrium is reached.
This means that the auto industry will be hit far sooner, and far harder, than a focus on just the VMT effect would suggest.
Crunching The Numbers There are 260 million cars, SUVs and light trucks currently on the road for personal use, give or take. This is actually more than one car per driver, but that is a whole separate issue I’ve already covered. My research shows that 18% of the population lives in rural areas, where I’ve already admitted ridesharing is unlikely to be practical. So that is 46.8 million vehicles - we’ll round to 47 million - that are going to stay in inventory exactly as they are now.
Among the urban/suburban group, 82% of the households in the US comes to about 94 million households. If these all became single-car households, all retaining car ownership but using Lyft and Uber to supplement when the family was not all traveling in the same direction, the inventory of cars in their homes would be 94 million, summing to 141 million total - roughly 120 million fewer cars than are in inventory now.
That is, by the way, a very conservative estimate. The latest surveys in my last articles show that 25% of the population already is at the point that they would be financially better off not owning any car and using Lyft and Uber for all their transportation needs. If we take 25% of the total away, inventory falls to 105 million cars, a 155 million unit drop.
But even that’s under-estimating, because Lyft and Uber are still growing . How far they will grow and exactly how much of the population they will come to engulf is still a matter of some conjecture. My analysis of suburban population trends showed that 63% of the population lived in just 3.5% of the land area of the country.
If we call that the true “urban” area where ridesharing can most easily take root, and say 80% of those people will eventually find it cheaper to share than to own, then 50% of the total population will not own any cars at the end of the transition period. That comes to 70 million cars in “personal inventory” and a 190 million unit drop.
Estimating A Timeframe The last step in our analysis is to set the length of time we believe the transition will take. I do not consider claims that it will be 2040 or 2050 before the transition is complete to be remotely accurate. In the first place, remember that essentially 0% of the population was better off swapping car-sharing for car-ownership four years ago, and now the number is already 25%, at least economically speaking.
In the second place, it behooves us to look at the rate of expansion of other technological leaps. Ten years ago Apple ( AAPL ) unveiled its first iPhone. No one would say it will take until 2040 for the smartphone to achieve its revolution. Ten years ago Netflix ( NFLX ) launched its first crummy streaming interface on its website. Now everyone is standing a death watch over the Pay-TV bundle.
Uber and Lyft are also already partly along in their transition - like I said, 25% of the population is already better off with them - so the question is not how long the transition takes in total but rather how much of the transition period is left. Opinions do vary, but somewhere between ten and twenty years is probably the most accurate.
Range Of Outcomes Rather than try to answer the question definitively, I’ve prepared the table below to show how different ownership levels and time lengths impact the inventory. The numbers in the chart represent "obviated sales" arising from shifts in inventory. The horizontal is the time length, the vertical is the remaining car ownership (inventory) level in the country.
10 years 15 years 20 years 141M 12M 8M 6M 105M 15.5M 10.33M 7.75M 70M 19M 12.67M 9.5M As you can see, the minimum impact is 6 million units a year, and the theoretical maximum could be as high as 19 million units a year in sales reductions. With the industry only selling 18 million units a year at its peak, that of course would be nothing less than, well, apocalyptic.
Now, I don’t expect it to get to 19 million units. But I would also say that 6 million units is probably too low. The midpoint estimate of a little over 10 million units would probably be my best estimate. Subtracted from the 18 million peak, that would put the industry’s average run rate over a fifteen-year period at 8 million units.
So far as my research has been able to determine, there is not a single automaker in the US, domestic or foreign, which claims to be able to turn a profit at an 8 million unit industry run rate.
Other Industries Affected The implications here go beyond the automakers, though obviously they’re at the very front of the firing line. As I indicated, banks like Citigroup, Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) and Wells Fargo ( WFC ) which finance large numbers of leases and car loans may suddenly find themselves with inventory they cannot easily liquidate. Also, the reduction in units being held has grave implications for auto insurance companies such as State Farm, Allstate ( ALL ) and Progressive ( PGR ) among others. Fewer cars means lower insurance premium payments.
As I indicated in my last article the impact on retailers will vary, with Amazon ( AMZN ) best placed to benefit as people with fewer cars purchase more products online for delivery right to their door. Walmart ( WMT ) and Target ( TGT ) are already launching delivery programs of their own as they try to adapt, while Costco ( COST ) is moving slower but has a strong membership program of its own to rival Prime and offers strong pricing. Walmart and Target are still trying to find a membership program that works.
All told, I’d call Amazon the only clear winner, with the others facing murky futures, as they try to ramp up delivery services fast enough to overcome declining brick-and-mortar operations
Avoid GM, And Ford As for the automakers themselves, they will all be hit hard if these projections are remotely accurate. Essentially, the midpoint of my estimate is that some 150 million units will disappear from inventory over a 15-year period. With Ford and GM constituting exactly one-third of auto sales in October 2017, and around that figure in most months, they come to 33.3% of the auto market. That means that they each have some 25 million cars they have already sold that they need to burn through before their replacement services are actually needed again.
I do not make claims about drastic shifts in industry norms lightly, and I don’t do it that often. But with respect to the other side, it does seem that a fundamental transformation is afoot in the auto sector. Lyft and Uber are drastically altering how we think about personal transportation and also how much capital and inventory needs to be tied up in providing it.
I believe we are continuing to underestimate the magnitude of the shift that is coming, and I recommend against any long positions in automakers despite their depressed P/E levels. This is not something investors should try to time, to squeeze every last dime of dividends out of what are, admittedly, still high-yielding stocks. At some point yields will collapse, and it’s not worth the risk to be the ones holding the stock when it does. I would avoid all auto stocks for now.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
